progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From p04: a blank zeroes the instrument; standards made by dilution; the linear range from the data; dilute an over-range unknown, remeasure, multiply back; read across then down; divide by the slope only when the line passes through zero; check accuracy with a standard of known value. From s06: concentration (the independent variable) along the bottom, absorbance up the side, even steps, small crosses, a line of best fit not dot to dot, read-off lines shown, "Inside the data, read it. Outside, doubt it." From c04 (route level): AAS measures a metal ion's concentration with a calibration. From chem-m5-p02: absorbance comes from the absorbing species; the blank sets zero. From s07: validity, reliability, accuracy. Year 11: mg/L as a concentration unit.
progression.startsWith: A calibration graph turns an absorbance into a concentration, but exam questions add a twist. The sample reads above the standards. The line doesn't start at zero. Or the result is right, but it's from the wrong sample for the question being asked. Here are three HSC-style questions on water samples. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.
progression.stopsAfter: plotting an AAS calibration graph with a line of best fit and read-off lines; explaining why an over-range sample is diluted rather than read from an extended line; calculating an original concentration through a dilution; explaining a non-zero intercept from a reagent blank and subtracting it before dividing by the slope; checking a quantification limit against a guideline; comparing results with a guideline; evaluating a claim that uses the wrong sample or too few samples.
progression.nextLesson: why monitor water and nutrient pollution? (route chem-m8-c05).

teaching.task: A calibration graph, a water sample and a guideline value: how do you turn an absorbance into a concentration you can defend, and decide what that concentration does and doesn't tell you about the water?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why concentration goes along the bottom: it was chosen (2b). Why dilute the sample: the line isn't known to be straight beyond the standards, and AAS lines can bend (2c). Why multiply by five: the instrument measured the diluted solution (2d). Why extending reads low here: the real response bends below the straight line (2e). Why the zero standard reads 0.032: it contains the reagent, and the zero was set with water (3b). Why subtract before dividing: 0.032 of every reading isn't iron (3c, 3d). Why check the quantification limit: a method must measure at the guideline's level to judge it (4b). Why the morning sample is higher: lead dissolves while water stands in the plumbing (4b). Why the claim fails: the flushed sample isn't the water drunk first, and one tap on one day isn't enough (4c). Why not average: the samples answer different questions (4d).
teaching.conversationalApproach: A calibration graph turns an absorbance into a concentration, but exam questions add a twist. Question one. Part a. Part b. Part c. The classic slip is extending the line up to point six two zero. Question two. Part a. Part b. The classic slip is dividing point two nine zero by the slope straight away. Question three. Start with the method. Now the claim. The trap is averaging the two results. So, for any calibration or monitoring question.

Or the result is right, but it's from the wrong sample for the question being asked. Here are three HSC-style questions on water samples. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a): Q1's full standards table, both absorbances, both volumes and an empty grid; Q2's reagent and zeroing conditions, the plotted line and its equation, the sample's absorbance; Q3's quantification limit, both samples with their times, the guideline value and the claim. Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the check strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope:
Syllabus dotpoints (as printed; NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, pp57 and 58; C8-IQ1-04 and C8-IQ1-01 are this project's local catalogue IDs, not codes printed in the syllabus), quoted from ../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y12.json:

"conduct investigations and/or process data to determine the concentration of coloured species and/or metal ions in aqueous solution, including but not limited to, the use of:
- colourimetry
- ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometry
- atomic absorption spectroscopy"

"analyse the need for monitoring the environment"

Practice and transfer only: first coverage of C8-IQ1-04 stays with chem-m8-c04 and chem-m8-p04; first coverage of C8-IQ1-01 is chem-m8-c05 and c06, which come after this video. G02's Q3 practises one narrow part of C8-IQ1-01 that needs no new teaching (judging one result against a guideline, and whether one sample is enough evidence); it does not teach why water is monitored, eutrophication, dissolved oxygen or BOD.

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in the G01 layout: top-left the question card (stem, data and demands as an exam prints them, with the tag "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience"), kept readable through each question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("AAS calibration with a dilution", "Colourimetry: a line with an intercept", "Judge the monitoring evidence"), hidden during each attempt because it names the method. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used. A check strip on the far left carries four rows, "inside the standards?", "every dilution?", "line starts at zero?", "right sample for the question?", and ticks the row each scene uses; it dims to an outline during every countdown. Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Colour key: copper blue, iron orange-red, lead slate grey; givens and units navy; the current answer bright; earlier lines dim; the linear range pale green; amber only for underlined givens. Clutter rule (owner): besides the question strip and the check strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; completed lines dim while the current line writes.

On "guideline" "0.012 mg L⁻¹" and "0.005 mg L⁻¹" underline; a slate marker "morning 0.012" lands right of the line; line "0.012 ÷ 0.005 = 2.4 × the guideline" (bright). On "under it" "0.002 mg L⁻¹" underlines and a second marker "flushed 0.002" lands left of the line. On "fittings" the time-of-day strip draws under the bar: "overnight: water stands in the pipes" (coded pipe outline, slate lead dots gathering) → "8 am: first drink" → "after 2 minutes: flushed" (dots flushed away). Strip: "right sample for the question?" lights (not yet ticked). Bright at the end: the two markers either side of the guideline and 2.4 ×.

scenes.visualReference: line "2.4 ×" dims; the bar stays. On "isn't the water" "Sample 2" in the claim underlines and the "flushed" marker dims; on "first drink" "first draw at 8 am" underlines and the "morning" marker pulses (tag "the water students drink first"). On "one bubbler" "one drinking bubbler" underlines; a coded row of five bubbler outlines appears, one filled, four grey with "?" (tag "one tap, one day"). Answer box writes in three short lines: "The claim is not supported: Sample 2 (flushed) is below the guideline, but Sample 1, the water drunk first each morning, is 2.4 times the guideline." / "Lead dissolves from the plumbing while water stands, so the result depends on when the sample is taken; one bubbler on one day can't show the water is safe." / "Before calling it safe: repeat sampling at every bubbler over several days, and advice from the local public health unit to find and control the lead source." On "source" the s07 FixRail flashes small ("feature: wrong sample, too few samples; fix: matching samples, repeated"). Strip: "right sample for the question?" ticks. Bright at the end: the answer box and the morning marker.
